After 3 months on Angular 2, a user loved it except for breaking changes across the RC series. They praised TypeScript, modular reusable components via @Input/@Output, HTML template directives (ngFor, ngIf) that designers can work with, and the built-in @angular/router.
A user who found Angular 2's UI libraries lacking: material2 was still in alpha and missing many components, which made it hard to quickly build a complete, good-looking UI.

Running Angular 2 in production since alpha.46: 3 web apps (20-60 components each) plus 3 Ionic 2 mobile apps. Highlights: truly reusable encapsulated components, third-party libs like D3 work without 'angularizing', readable (events)/[attributes] syntax, great performance, friendly community, AOT and tree-shaking.

Evaluated React vs Angular 2 and picked React. Angular templates stored in strings got no editor coloring, intellisense or tag matching. Typos in {{variables}} produced no compile-time or runtime error, just missing output. Also no refactoring support and ngFor syntax to learn, versus React's checked JSX.
Angular's module syntax makes version-control merge conflicts very easy, even easier than import statements.
A user on Angular 1 who would pick React next: Angular 'just stranded all their developers' with the 2.0 rewrite, while React has a big head start on mindshare, plugins and tutorials.

On a large AngularJS app, the team hit pitfalls about 7 months in. Workarounds: one-way binding (bindonce) to reduce watchers, careful use of $apply/$digest, ng-boilerplate scaffolding, custom style guides, and frequent code reviews.

Building complex views in AngularJS, a user hit performance problems with large tables. The $digest dirty-checking slows to a crawl after about 8k-10k bindings; workarounds were one-time binding, infinite scroll, or rendering less. They also struggled with transclusion and isolate scopes, and wouldn't have chosen it knowing Angular 2 broke compatibility.
A user built a fairly complex app (SlimWiki) with Angular and had 'nothing but great experiences'. The main issue: no guidelines on right/wrong ways to do things, so it needs to be more opinionated.

Using Angular professionally since 2012: it's flexible enough for typical CRUD apps and enjoyable. But the provider system is poorly documented, third-party libraries are of middling quality, best practices aren't presented anywhere, and the framework source is hard to debug.

A user's AngularJS selling points: easy testing with Karma, Protractor and DI; very fast development; lots of books and directives; easy integration of jQuery plugins. Drawbacks: needs serious JS knowledge, has performance issues, and is overhyped.

A SaaS built on Angular with about 170 views, 70 directives and 100 controllers. Performance dropped in places but was fixable through benchmarking; the key was loading directives when needed and destroying them afterwards. No serious issues found so far.
One-and-a-half-year Angular user: the only issue is pages with large data bindings. The Angular team's answer of 'don't do that' is unacceptable and their silence has been frustrating.

A Google engineer has used AngularJS for 3 years. Bad parts: the directives API, global injector namespacing, and watch counts. Still, Google has shared reusable directive components and >3-year-old, >100k SLOC apps without major maintenance issues when the style guide is followed.
A user who tested TypeScript with Angular had a positive experience, and was glad Angular moved to TypeScript instead of forking it for AtScript annotations.
A user's comparison: React's learning curve is tiny next to Angular's, at about 5 component methods and 1-2 top-level APIs, and 'it's just JavaScript'.

Angular 2 performance numbers are impressive: optimized code renders about 2x faster than other frameworks, and unoptimized code is on par with optimized React. Tooling maturity is still the greater pain point, says a user on the Angular side who prefers declarative templates.
A user prefers Angular over React: it's opinionated so less time is wasted on decisions, MVC organization is simpler, (click)="onSelect()" is easier than binding in React, and HTML stays out of JS.
The Angular 2 router (beta) needed much more work. Passing data to child routes, getting current route segments, and checking the active route were not easily possible.

Angular 2 template syntax like *ngFor="#hero of heroes" and [title]/(close) is invalid HTML and XML. That rules out existing HTML editors, validators and generators for templates, with no tangible benefit in return.
